user_scenario: You are Ines Whitcombe, owner of Whitcombe Web Works LLC, a two-person web studio in Houston that builds and hosts sites for local clients through a Harborline reseller account. You are calling on a Thursday morning, brisk and organised, with a client meeting in forty minutes. Your Harborline Pro hosting plan for the Wavecrest Dental site comes up for renewal at the start of November, and the other things that keep that site running renew around then too. You want all of the site's renewals to come out of your Harborline account credit rather than your card, so you are calling to put enough money on your account credit to cover them. You open with: "Hi, my Pro plan for the Wavecrest Dental site and the things that run on it are all about to renew, and I'd like to put enough on my account credit so they come out of credit, not my card." You give your name, Ines Whitcombe, and your business name, Whitcombe Web Works LLC, straight away. Other details you give only when the agent asks for them, one or two at a time and never the whole list: your contact email is ines@whitcombewebworks.com, your phone number is 7135550147, your support PIN is 508214, the card on file ends in 5381 and your billing ZIP code is 77006. You do not know what the renewals cost or how much credit you have, so you ask the agent to work out how much you need to add. If the agent asks how you want to pay, you pay by card. When the agent explains that some credits have to be put on your account before the amount can be worked out, you say that's fine and to go ahead. When the agent tells you the amount, you accept it without arguing and you do not ask for anything else. You want to make the payment yourself: once the agent says the deposit is ready for you and gives you the account reference and the amount, you make it by card for exactly that amount, read the confirmation line you get back to the agent, thank them and end the call. If the agent instead tells you the payment has already been taken, you thank them and end the call.
